segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We said that the word for always was siempre.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Now, if you know Italian or some other Latin language, maybe you have something like sempre in that language, and you can see again that the E is splitting between sempre and siempre. So if you know one of these other languages or if you've studied them, it can be useful just to notice that, and just noticing that helps you internalize this new word. So, for example,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: well in Spanish is bien, like in the beginning of welcome, bienvenido. This in Italian is bene. We see that we get rid of the E, the last E, and the E in the middle splits. You have from French, bon for good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What do you think good might be in Spanish? What do you think we'll do to make that more Spanish?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We also said that vamos, vamos meant we're going or let's go, and it's something that you're going to hear all the time. ¡Vamos, vamos, let's go!

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, another useful skill that we want in language learning is to work backwards, not just to work from the to form, take off the -ar or the -er or the -ir and add bits on, but we want to get in the habit of also working backwards, because maybe we see or hear somewhere a word like vamos, and we want to be able to work backwards from vamos to get the other versions, taking off the ending which is for we and putting our other bits on.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, could you work out from vamos how it would be he goes or is going, she goes or is going, you formal go or are going?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: The thing is you don't know the ending of the to form.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: If you have -amos, you know which is your vowel, no?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ah, yes. Okay, yes. So, va?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Va. What does that mean, va?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: He, she, it, or you formal...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you make that you informal?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: If you want to say where are you going, you will hear to where are you going. What was the word for to?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: A. So, how would you say to where, to where are you going?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What would be they go or you plural go?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, we can work backwards: vamos, va, vas, van. What was the I version? It was irregular and we remembered it by thinking I'm going on a voyage?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, the to form, to go, is ir. I-R, all by itself. Ir.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, it's it's very irregular, and this is actually because this verb is two verbs that kind of stuck together to form one verb over time.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So in French, you have like aller, no, which means going, and in English we get alleyway from this, and alleyway is like a road, no? And this is related to ir.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So ir comes from one verb historically, and then the versions of ir actually come from a different verb.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, they kind of stuck together over time and they give us this very irregular situation. That's just for interest, we don't need to know any of this. All we need to know is voy, from voyage, and vamos, and we can work backwards from vamos, and there we have the complete set: voy, vamos, va, vas, van. But to go is ir.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: They are coming from two different verbs historically, which is why we have ir, which is an -ir verb, but A coming up for all of the different versions. So, how would you say I want to go?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. I can go. I have the power to go.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Debo ir. I have to go. So, not I must go, debo ir, I have to go. What is I have, from tener?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tengo. And what do we add to that to get the meaning of have to?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Que. Like I said, there's no comfortable translation for it, but we add on que to tengo, and we get the feeling of have to rather than the feeling of possession. So, I have to go?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tengo que ir. I have to go now.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. The word for tonight is this night: esta noche. Esta noche. So, I have to go tonight, I have to go this night?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, noche is feminine. We know this because esta, the word for this, is ending in an A. So, how would you say the night?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: La noche. So, we said that words ending A are feminine, or there are feminine endings like -ción or -idad: la opinión, la oportunidad. If it ends in an E, there's actually no way of knowing whether it's masculine or feminine by the word. You have to look at what's around it. Or in the dictionary it will tell you. But if you hear it in conversation, you have a look at what's around it: esta noche, and then you can go, "Oh, okay, so noche is feminine."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Another example of a feminine word that ends in an E is carne. Carne. What do you think carne means? It's not at all obvious. You have carnage in English. It was just carnage. Carne is meat.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Meat. And it's a feminine word. So, the meat?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: La carne. I don't eat meat?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No como carne. The word for and in Spanish is y, and it's just spelled with a Y by itself: y.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: I don't eat meat and I don't drink, or I don't take, alcohol. So, tomar was to take, tomar, and comer, to eat. So, how would you say I don't eat meat and I don't take alcohol, I don't drink alcohol?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Alcohol, good, 'cause we don't pronounce H in Spanish, do we? No como carne y no tomo alcohol. Or if you wanted to say I eat meat and I take alcohol, I eat meat and I drink alcohol, how would that be?
